top_level_objectives: Observe and describe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars against the background stars from Earth’s perspective.
Explain retrograde motion using the relative motion of Earth and Mars in a heliocentric model.
Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and relate their differing sizes to orbital distance and speed.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the observational puzzle by showing Mars over several weeks as it drifts among the constellations.
key_visuals: A dark Earth-based night sky with recognizable background stars and constellation lines
Mars highlighted as it shifts position night to night along the ecliptic
A simple date progression showing the change across several weeks
student_actions: Observe Mars’s changing position over time
Identify the general eastward drift before the reversal
Predict when the motion might appear to slow or switch direction

scenes.scene_name: The Retrograde Loop as Seen from Earth
scenes.brief_purpose: Present the full retrograde event so students can see the temporary westward loop that Mars makes against the stars.
key_visuals: Mars tracing a short loop or hook-shaped path across the star field
A timeline marking the onset, peak, and end of retrograde motion
Constellation landmarks that make the shift in direction easy to track
student_actions: Follow Mars’s path through the loop
Notice the change from eastward motion to westward motion and back again
Describe the loop in words as an apparent motion rather than a true planetary reversal

scenes.brief_purpose: Contrast the older geocentric explanation with the more accurate heliocentric one to frame the historical puzzle.
key_visuals: A simplified geocentric sketch with Mars’s loop represented as a complicated path
A side-by-side heliocentric sketch showing smoother planetary motion
Visual emphasis on how each model accounts for the same observation
student_actions: Compare how each model explains the observed loop
Identify which explanation is more natural and why
Reflect on why the observation challenged older cosmic models

scenes.scene_name: Viewing the Solar System from Outside
scenes.brief_purpose: Show Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun so students can connect the apparent loop to real orbital motion.
key_visuals: A solar-system view with the Sun centered and Earth on an inner orbit, Mars on an outer orbit
Earth moving faster than Mars along its path
A line of sight from Earth to Mars sweeping across the background
student_actions: Watch Earth overtake Mars on the inside track
Trace how the Earth-Mars line of sight shifts during the encounter
Link the changing line of sight to the apparent backward motion seen from Earth

scenes.brief_purpose: Use a familiar everyday analogy to reinforce the relative-motion idea behind retrograde motion.
key_visuals: Two cars on adjacent lanes, with the faster car overtaking the slower one
The slower car seeming to drift backward from the driver’s viewpoint
A brief visual bridge back to Earth and Mars
student_actions: Relate the car analogy to the Earth-Mars system
Explain why an object can appear to move backward without actually reversing direction
Use the analogy to check their understanding of apparent motion

scenes.scene_name: Retrograde Motion of Jupiter and Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the concept by comparing Mars with the more subtle retrograde loops of Jupiter and Saturn.
key_visuals: Separate orbital views of Jupiter and Saturn compared with Mars
Smaller, less dramatic retrograde loops for the outer planets
A visual cue showing increasing orbital distance from the Sun
student_actions: Compare loop size and timing among the planets
Notice that more distant planets show smaller retrograde effects
Summarize how orbital speed and distance influence the appearance of retrograde motion
